reason: It leaves temporary directories and configuration files behind because its cleanup never deletes them.
It checks meaningful fallbacks, column limits, and rendered content that realistic bugs would break, and creates nothing requiring cleanup.
It pins incidental help and display wording while leaving doctor behavior and successful recent-message argument forwarding untested.
It checks known luminance values and both gamma branches, would catch incorrect weights or conversion math, and creates no files.
It pins incidental sign-in wording and never triggers a genuine exception to check the function's error handling.

It runs the real function in a temp sandbox and checks the fixed-location order, PATH lookup of a real executable, and the null result. It restores PATH and the fs mock and deletes its temp dir, and the two surviving mutations look like equivalent mutants in the shell-lookup guards.

It runs the real function in an isolated temp folder, checks exact file contents and JSON results for map-ref healing, empty-section removal, a dry run that writes nothing, and an empty workspace, and cleans up after itself; the surviving mutants are in the untested human-readable output path.

It runs answerWish against a temp home with a stubbed dispatcher, checks the answer text, the dispatch arguments and the saved record, and checks that error cases leave the wishes file unchanged. It does not cover picking the newest waiting wish or the stale-question refusal, but those are covered by test/wish.test.js.

It runs the real function in a temp workspace and checks real behavior: dry runs write nothing, custom files are kept unless forced, and an unreadable destination throws, with env and files cleaned up. The one gap is that no case passes a non-default workspace_template, which is likely how the one mutation survived.
It catches incorrect ledger paths and ignored environment overrides, checks for unwanted file creation, restores the environment, and removes its temporary directories.
It checks parsed contents and missing or malformed file handling, catches realistic loading bugs, and restores the environment and removes temporary files.
It checks useful command classifications but hardcodes the diagnostic wording, so harmless message edits would fail the test.
It catches realistic bugs in saved sleep settings, loop isolation, argument parsing, and corrupt-state recovery, and cleans up its temporary files.
It checks wiki path selection but duplicates the entire prompt, so harmless wording or formatting edits would fail it.

It checks the 16-hex-character format that startedLine requires and that tokens are unique across calls, so a constant, short or non-hex token would fail it, and it touches no files, network or timing.

It drives the real msgCommand with only auth and the API mocked, and checks argv slicing, joined message text, the exact requests sent, the help-anywhere usage exit, the empty-conversation read path (no mark-as-read call), and the rejected-send error and exit code. It cleans up its temp home, env, argv and module cache, and it covers the msgCommand wrapper and error paths that the older socialCommand tests don't.
The second test usefully checks that help flags win over --all/--check and return 0 without touching a repo, but the first test pins exact help-text lines that any harmless wording edit would break.

It runs the real function against an isolated temp home and checks outcomes callers rely on: XP totals and level, a linked receipt chain, no duplicate awards on replay, ineligible episodes skipped, a half-written final line resumed once completed, and bad JSON throwing without writing files. It cleans up everything it creates.

It only checks the help screen, pinning exact help wording with regexes, and never tests the card, the JSON output or the `--as` option, though it does confirm that `-h`, `help` and `--json --help` all print the same help and return 0.
It creates temporary directories and files but never cleans them up.
It largely repeats existing billing tests and pins exact wording and punctuation that harmless edits would change.

It checks real behavior callers rely on (directories created, only paths and base_commit persisted, a second save overwrites the first, a blocking file throws and is left intact) and cleans up its temp folders. The exact-string checks pin the JSON indent and trailing newline, but the parsed-content checks sit beside them and cover the same behavior.
It catches ignored home overrides, broken fallback behavior, and bypassed home protection using isolated paths, and it restores its mock and removes temporary files.
It creates temporary home directories and JSON files without ever deleting them.
It checks campaign-specific paths and side-effect-free lookup, would catch incorrect routing or unexpected disk writes, and cleans up its temporary directories.

It runs real git in a temp repo and checks what callers rely on: directory expansion that skips tracked, ignored and outside files, filenames with spaces, tabs, newlines and unicode, and an empty list when git can't read the repo. It would fail on realistic bugs like dropping `-z` or `--exclude-standard`. It isolates HOME and the git config, restores the environment, and removes its temp folder.
It checks exact commit identity, updates after new commits, and null error results using real Git repositories, then restores the environment and removes its temporary files.

It checks the journal helpers that log syncing relies on, including the 5 millisecond timestamp edge, the content fingerprint, section order, and conflict handling, using only in-memory calls with correct expected values, though one parse check pins a dropped trailing newline.

The handoff-chaining test checks real behavior, but the other tests assert the whole prompt string, including a verbatim copy of the approval rule and a stray trailing space, and the last one asserts an accidental TypeError. gm-bet.test.js already covers the handoff and approval lines.

It calls answerMissionHumanAsk directly against a temp ledger and checks the saved answer, the audit event, the legacy string-ask path, the refusal to answer twice, and that bad answers or indices leave the ledger unchanged and write no event, which the CLI-level test elsewhere doesn't cover; it isolates HOME and env and removes its temp folder, with only the error message wording slightly over-pinned.
It catches broken permission restrictions and uniquely checks all four hook commands without creating files or depending on external state.

It checks each branch of loginToken (explicit token skips lookup, credential fallback, empty string on missing, empty or error results, lookup errors propagate) through injected dependencies, with no real home folder, network or leftover files, and no other test covers the function.
It catches realistic actor filtering, normalization, deduplication, and fallback bugs through concrete assertions and creates no files or external dependencies.

It directly tests the human-only gate that campaign-core, campaign-lanes and the schedule command rely on, covers case, whitespace, prefix position and non-string inputs, and has no side effects, though pinning 'human:' as true is a slightly debatable choice.

It runs the real query against in-memory SQLite and checks the since-boundary, workspace filtering, ordering by task and version, the claimed-task union without duplicates, and the empty case. It leaves no files behind, and no other test covers this function.
It checks useful rendering behavior but pins exact wording, separators, and title width that harmless presentation edits could change.
It catches realistic errors in row ordering, limits, club grouping, and missing member handling without creating files or relying on external state.

It covers the skill-create success paths (local flag, customer folder, description with '=', integration template) that no other test covers, and it isolates cwd and HOME and cleans up; it pins some template and message wording.
It catches realistic sorting, filtering, limit, and input mutation bugs using fixed in-memory data without creating files or depending on the machine.

It checks the real slug rules that name the saved receipt files for the learn, x-search and youtube callers (lowercasing, collapsing separators, the 48-character cap, the 'query' fallback), it has no other test covering this, and it touches no files, network or clock. One weakness: it also pins two odd edge cases, the trailing dash left after cutting to 48 characters and 0 becoming 'query'.
It checks meaningful outcome branches, but every assertion pins exact prose, spacing, and punctuation that harmless presentation changes would break.
It asserts that requesting zero lines returns every line, locking in a slice(-0) bug as correct behavior.

It tests a pure function with no files or I/O, covers both the ignored and counted path patterns (including anchor edges, whitespace trimming and empty input), would fail if a pattern were loosened or dropped, and no other test file covers it.
It checks a missing title but would also fail on harmless changes to the prompt label or quotation formatting.
It pins exact error wording and never verifies that the parsed filter is actually used.

It checks that '24:00' is rejected, which fails if the hour upper bound on line 69 is loosened. It matches only a loose 'invalid time' message, touches no files, network or machine state, and no other test covers rejecting out-of-range 24-hour times.

It runs the real loop against a fake CLI that would normally finish the mission, then checks that the no-complete option keeps the mission open and never calls complete. Removing that check on line 325 would fail it, no other test covers this, and it restores HOME and deletes its temp folder.

It builds a real temp workspace with a journal entry and checks that the matching line shows up in compact search output, which fails if the journal-hits check is flipped. The assertion is on the matched content, not incidental wording, and the temp folder is cleaned up.

It checks a real behavior (on Linux with lsof missing, an engine is matched to the workspace through its /proc cwd), it fails if the Linux branch condition is broken, it uses only injected fakes plus a temp dir, and it restores platform, HOME and cwd and removes the temp dir.

It checks a real rule: a lead pinned to one model is judged only on that model's runs, so another model's successes can't hide its failures. I traced the setup by hand: it passes on the current code, and it would fail if the model filter or the recent-runs window were dropped. It uses in-memory data only, and no other roster-suggest test covers this case.

It closes a loop on Jan 10, renders the page as of Jan 15, and asserts the loop is absent from the 'closed or shipped today' list. That fails if line 52 stops checking the closed day, it holds in any timezone, and it cleans up its temp folder and its HOME and console changes.

It drives a real drafted-then-emptied beat through start, syncStates and readPlan in a temp folder, checks that the plan returns to empty (a case write.test.js doesn't cover), and restores HOME, cwd and console.log with the temp folder removed at exit.

It deletes a discovered skill folder before packaging and checks that the build still writes the plugin file, which fails if the directory guard is removed (the copy would throw on the missing folder). It uses a temp home and working folder, restores state, and no other plugin test covers this case.

It mocks the owner-engine lookup and the ask runner, then checks that the owner and workspace are passed through and the picked engine and model reach the ask job and the draft; nothing else in test/ covers this path, and it cleans up its temp folder.

It runs real planLayout input through the items-to-columns conversion and asserts the headings for both string and object items, which would catch a realistic mapping bug, with no files, timing or machine dependence, though it leaves the sub/body text and the 4-item cap unchecked.
It is correct, isolated and cleans up after itself, but test/todo--mut-L35-0.test.js already checks that a claimed database task lands in inProgress, so it adds no new coverage.

It covers the documented 'check file is still there' rule, which no other test exercises. Removing the onBase check would make it fail, because the file was added on a side branch, merged, then deleted. It builds a real git repo in a temp folder, restores HOME, and cleans up through the clean-temp helper.

It drives the real interactive log prompt with a fake terminal and typed '  ExIt  ', and asserts the 'saved' confirmation appears, which fails if exit stops being trimmed and case-insensitive. It uses a temp home that gets cleaned up and restores everything it patches.

It does check that a 200 reply to the spa PATCH gives no warning, which the older spa test doesn't, but it also pins every log line and the full request sequence, so a harmless wording edit would break it.

It fakes a failing git diff (exit 128) and checks that the deploy reports the error, returns 1 and never pushes, which fails if the status check on line 574 is dropped; it uses no network, and it restores HOME and the working folder and removes the temp folders it makes.

It checks that an explicit page title wins over the brand name in the rendered <title> tag, which callers rely on. No other test covers that, it would fail if the order were swapped or opts.title ignored, and it creates no files and uses no network.

It checks a behavior callers rely on, that double-quoted and single-quoted flag values lose their surrounding quotes in both the separated and inline forms. No other test covers this, it would fail if either quote branch were broken, and it touches no files, network or home folder. It doesn't test mismatched or unquoted values, but that gap is minor.

It forces a real spawn failure by pointing process.execPath at a missing file, then checks that the Node error message reaches both the JSON report and the saved receipt, which fails if line 241's fallback order changes. It restores process.execPath and console.log and deletes its temp folder. The one weak spot is that it pins Node's exact 'spawnSync … ENOENT' wording.

It checks that a caller's custom description reaches the description field of the generated member file, and it would fail on realistic mutations like always using the default text. No other test in test/ checks a custom description, it creates no files, and it parses the field instead of pinning exact formatting.
It verifies that callers receive the claimed task's original title, catches title loss or corruption, adds coverage absent from existing tests, and creates no files.

It runs a real `git init` in a temp repo, saves an idea from a subfolder, and checks it lands in the repo-root inbox, so it fails if the git-top lookup breaks. It pins no wording, sets HOME to a temp folder and restores it, and the clean-temp helper deletes the folders.

It drives the real interactive accent prompt with a stubbed readline, enters '2blue', and checks the saved accent stays the first swatch (#B5572E). That fails if the numeric-prefix guard on line 87 is loosened, since '2blue' would then pick swatch 2. It uses a temp folder, restores all globals, and cleans up through the clean-temp helper.

It runs the real dream command with a stand-in model that returns garbage and a fixed timestamp, then checks that the 'no dreams' note saved to disk carries that exact timestamp, which no other dream test checks. It would fail if the note used the current time instead. It gives the same result every run, puts back everything it changes, and its temp folder is deleted afterward.

The test passes even with line 39 removed, because the null entry is already rejected by `entry &&` on line 38 and primitives fail the verdict check, so it doesn't pin what it claims; it only guards the null case, which is correct and clean but adds little.

It uses mock timers (no real waiting) and a temp folder it removes, and it checks that following a running receipt prints only the new log bytes at exactly the requested interval, so ignoring or changing pollMs would fail the 36-then-37 tick check.

It checks that a blocker task title keeps the real stop reason in plain words ('runner failed'), which no other test in test/ checks. It uses a temp folder, restores HOME, deletes the folder and injects fakes so nothing touches the network or real home, but it does not exercise the 'blocked' fallback on line 120.

It runs the no-subject interview in a temp workspace, with the process spawn mocked and HOME and cwd restored afterward. It checks the operator mode, the loaded context file and the exit code, and it would fail if line 186 stopped treating the default 'me' as the operator. The temp folder is cleaned up by the clean-temp helper.

It tests a real caller-facing rule (an explicit html format with a text-only body is refused without render proof) that no other test covers, because the existing tests pass a body file, which triggers the gate on its own. It matches only the stable error id, isolates HOME and TMPDIR, restores process.exit and console.error, and the clean-temp helper removes its temp folder.
Existing YouTube tests already check these path conventions, while the extra cases pin incidental behavior for empty, missing, or malformed arguments.
It checks local midnight rounding and input preservation with fixed dates, catches realistic bugs, and creates nothing to clean up.
It catches realistic mission filtering and case handling bugs in the awake roster using fixed timestamps and creates nothing requiring cleanup.
It checks useful scanning and saving behavior, but exact help text and report wording make harmless copy edits fail.
It verifies model family and version captures callers rely on, adds malformed-name coverage, and catches inconsistent repeated matching without side effects.
It pins exact help and refusal wording and mostly repeats approval checks already covered by another test.
It catches realistic grouping, scoring, and finished-job counting bugs, covers malformed inputs, and cleans up its temporary directory.
It catches incorrect scorecard data, builder attribution, review enrichment and duplicate writes, and removes its temporary files.
It verifies actual directory changes and cases that must stay put, catches broken redirect logic, restores process settings, and removes its temporary files.

It pins the exact wording of a help-text constant and asserts that calling a string throws a TypeError, which tests JavaScript rather than this code. Only the taskProofState and executed-proof checks on the example say anything real, and it also overwrites HOME and deletes ATRIS_ environment variables without restoring them.

It runs real git in throwaway temp folders and checks the HEAD hash and dirty-file set across clean, dirty, committed, no-commit, staged, renamed, non-repo, missing-path and null cases. A bug in the status parsing or the error fallbacks would fail it, and every folder it makes is removed.

It runs the real entry point (reading process.argv) with a faked API, checks the exact request bodies, exit codes and error paths, uses a temp home folder, and cleans up; some output wording is pinned and several cases overlap test/social-command.test.js.
It repeats existing version and JSON rejection coverage and pins exact error wording that harmless edits could change.
It asserts that node --check plainword references no file, preserving a bug that misses valid extensionless scripts.

It runs the real cloudAtris wrapper and checks exit codes, stdout vs stderr, help flags winning over a broken business file, and unknown-subcommand and no-business errors failing before any network call, which no other test covers; it also cleans up its temp folders and uses a fake HOME. Its one weakness is pinning the exact help and error text.
It pins the exact empty-queue message, so a harmless wording change would fail the test.
It mostly pins incidental greeting and prompt text already covered elsewhere, while leaving live task dispatch and execution untested.
